title: I DON'T WRITE TO IMPRESS PEOPLE. I WRITE BECAUSE SOMEWHERE, SOMEONE IS ONE PRAYER AWAY FROM GIVING UP.
paragraphs: I DON'T WRITE TO IMPRESS PEOPLE. I WRITE BECAUSE SOMEWHERE, SOMEONE IS ONE PRAYER AWAY FROM GIVING UP.

I never know how long the message will be. Sometimes I don't even know what I'm going to write about. But before my fingers touch the keyboard, I surrender one thing to the Holy Spirit: Lord, let these words reach the person who needs to find Jesus today.
There is something I need to tell you about every article I write.
Something you may never have noticed.

And perhaps, after reading this, you will understand why some of my messages are longer than you expected. Why certain words seem to touch wounds you have never spoken about. Why sometimes you find yourself reading something you weren't even looking for, only to discover that it speaks directly to a battle you have been fighting in silence.
I cannot tell you that every person who reads my articles will experience something extraordinary.
But I can tell you what happens before I write them.
I pray.
Not for popularity.
Not for applause.
Not for another article that people will praise and forget tomorrow.
I pray for someone I may never meet.
Someone who might be crying behind a locked bathroom door while everyone else thinks they are doing fine.
Someone who has been attending church for years but has quietly begun wondering whether God still hears them.
Someone who has fallen into the same sin again and is ashamed to lift their eyes toward heaven.
Someone whose marriage is breaking.
Someone whose faith is exhausted.
Someone who still believes in Jesus but no longer knows how to find their way back to Him.
And sometimes, someone who doesn't believe in Jesus at all.
Someone who has been wounded by religion, disappointed by Christians, or convinced that God could never love a person with their history.
I don't know their name.
I don't know their address.
I don't know what happened to them last night.
But my prayer remains the same.
"Holy Spirit, please guide me. Let whatever I write be faithful to Your Word. And if there is even one person who needs to hear this message, Lord, please let it reach them."
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior.
And perhaps you are beginning to understand why I don't always know how long an article will be.
Because when I sit down to write, I don't want my own preferences to have the final word.
I want to surrender my plans, my thoughts, my timing, and my words to the Lord.
Sometimes a message comes together in a few paragraphs.
Sometimes it grows into something much longer.

Sometimes I begin with one Scripture and discover that I need to examine another passage, pray again, reconsider a sentence, or remove something that sounds powerful but isn't faithful to what the Bible actually says.
I don't want to force an ending simply because people have short attention spans.
And I don't want to make a message longer simply because longer writing might keep someone on a screen.
The length is not sacred.
The message must be faithful.
And the One I want to honor is Jesus Christ.
But there is something important I must make clear.
Surrendering my writing to the Holy Spirit does not mean that every sentence I write is a direct revelation from God.
I am not an apostle writing another book of Scripture.
I am not claiming that my personal impressions carry the authority of the Bible.
I am a servant who needs grace, correction, discernment, and the truth of God's Word just as much as anyone reading my articles.
The Holy Spirit never needs me to exaggerate His work to make Him appear powerful.
His Word is already powerful.
And that brings me to a passage that has shaped how I understand this responsibility.
In John 16:13, Jesus describes the Holy Spirit as:
τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας
to pneuma tēs alētheias
"The Spirit of truth."
That Greek expression matters.
Jesus did not describe the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of emotional excitement, religious popularity, or impressive storytelling.
He called Him the Spirit of truth.

In the same passage, Jesus explains that the Spirit will guide His disciples into the truth. And in John 16:14, He says something that I believe every Christian writer, preacher, teacher, and content creator needs to remember.
"He shall glorify me." — John 16:14, KJV
Read that again.
He shall glorify Me.
Jesus.
Not the writer.
Not the ministry.
Not the person holding the microphone.
Not the number of followers.
Not the name printed at the bottom of an article.
Jesus Christ.
If my writing makes people admire my words but never leads them to consider the Savior, I have missed the very purpose of Gospel Warrior.
If people remember my name but forget the cross, something has gone terribly wrong.
If my articles stir emotions but never point toward repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and transformation through Christ, then beautiful writing is not enough.
Because the Holy Spirit does not exist to build my reputation.
He glorifies Jesus.
And that is why, whatever subject I write about, I want the message to find its way back to Christ.
A broken marriage?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A hidden addiction?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A painful betrayal?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A warning against hypocrisy?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A testimony of restoration?
Jesus must remain at the center.

Even when the subject is uncomfortable, even when the truth exposes something we would rather hide, even when the article makes someone angry before it makes them think, my desire is not to win an argument.
It is to remain faithful to the Gospel.
Because without Jesus, Gospel Warrior would become just another page filled with inspirational words.
And the world already has enough inspiration that cannot save a soul.
There is a difference between feeling better for five minutes and being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
One can happen through an encouraging sentence.
The other happens only through the Savior who died for our sins and rose again.
And I never want to confuse the two.
Sometimes I think about the person who almost scrolls past one of my articles.
Maybe they see the length and think, "That's too much to read."
I understand.
Life is busy.
People are tired.
Our minds are constantly pulled in a hundred directions.
But somewhere inside that long message may be a Scripture they have never understood, a truth they have avoided, or a reminder of God's mercy they desperately need.
I cannot promise that every article will be for every person.
I cannot promise that the Holy Spirit personally dictated every word.
But I can pray that God will use whatever is true, faithful, and helpful in the writing to accomplish good beyond anything I could plan.
And I can trust Him with what happens after I publish.
That trust is rooted in Scripture.
Isaiah 55:11 says:
"So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it." — KJV
The Hebrew word translated "void" is רֵיקָם (rēqām), carrying the sense of emptiness or without accomplishing its intended purpose.
Notice whose word God is speaking about.
His Word.
Not every thought that enters my mind.
Not every emotional sentence I write.
Not every article simply because I attach a Bible verse to it.
God's Word accomplishes His purposes.
That is precisely why I want Scripture to shape my writing rather than merely decorate it.
I want to understand what a passage meant in its original context before applying it to someone's present struggle.
I want to handle Hebrew and Greek carefully, not use ancient words to create an impression of spiritual authority.
I want to distinguish what the Bible actually promises from what I personally hope will happen.
Because the person reading may be holding on to every word.
And when someone is spiritually wounded, careless words can do real harm.
I think about that often.
Imagine a woman sitting alone after midnight.
She has spent years trying to keep her family together.
She smiles at church.
She tells everyone she is blessed.
But behind closed doors, she feels invisible.
She opens Facebook, not because she is looking for a sermon, but because she wants a few minutes of distraction.
Then she sees an article about the Samaritan woman at the well.
She reads how Jesus knew the complicated details of that woman's life and still chose to speak with her.
For the first time in months, she remembers that being fully known by Christ does not mean being beyond His reach.
Or imagine a man who has spent years pretending that his secret sin is under control.
He has made promises.
Broken them.
Made them again.
He has become skilled at hiding his struggle from everyone except himself.
Then he reads about Peter.
The disciple who insisted he would never deny Jesus.
The disciple who failed so publicly.
The disciple who wept bitterly.
And later, the disciple whom the risen Christ restored and commissioned.
Perhaps that man finally realizes that repentance is not the same as hopelessness.
That his sin must not be excused.
But neither must he conclude that his failure is greater than the mercy of Christ.
These are examples, not stories I claim to have personally witnessed.
But they represent the kinds of human struggles that lead me to pray over every message.
Because behind every profile picture is a real person.
Behind every reaction is a life we cannot fully see.
Behind some of the loudest smiles are prayers nobody has heard.
And behind some of the quietest accounts are people desperately trying to survive another day.
That is why I refuse to think of Gospel Warrior as merely a content page.
To me, it is a responsibility.
A place where the Scriptures must be handled with reverence.
A place where broken people should hear both the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's grace.
A place where the comfortable can be challenged without being treated with contempt.
A place where the wounded can find compassion without being given false promises.
A place where seekers can ask difficult questions without being mocked.
And a place where every road leads back to the Person at the center of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ.
Paul expressed this priority in 1 Corinthians 2:2:
"For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." — KJV
Paul was not saying that Christians should never discuss other subjects.
He was declaring the central importance of the crucified Christ in his ministry.
The Greek phrase Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν καὶ τοῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον (Iēsoun Christon kai touton estaurōmenon) emphasizes Jesus Christ as the One crucified.
That is the center.
Not motivational slogans.
Not religious performance.
Not a personality cult built around a Christian creator.
The crucified and risen Savior.
And this is where my heart becomes especially burdened.
Because I know how easy it is for Christian content to become another form of entertainment.
We read something powerful.
We feel convicted.
We react with a heart emoji.
We say, "Amen."
Then we continue living exactly as before.
But the Gospel calls us to more than momentary emotion.
It calls us to repentance and faith.
To surrender.
To obedience.
To loving God and our neighbor.
To forgiving because we have been forgiven.
To turning away from sin, not merely feeling guilty about it.
To becoming disciples who follow Jesus even when nobody is watching.
James 1:22 says:
"But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." — KJV
That verse confronts me as a writer too.
Because I can write about forgiveness and still need to forgive someone.
I can write about humility and still need to repent of pride.
I can write about trusting God and still struggle with fear.
I can write about surrender and discover another area of my life I have been trying to control.
I am not standing above the people who read Gospel Warrior.
I am standing with them beneath the authority of the same Word.
And I need Jesus every single day.
That is something I never want you to forget.
The Gospel Warrior is not the hero of these stories.
Jesus is.
The Gospel Warrior is not the one who can forgive your sins.
Jesus is.
The Gospel Warrior cannot heal every wound, restore every relationship, or guarantee that your suffering will end tomorrow.
But I can keep pointing you to the One who conquered sin and death, who receives repentant sinners, and who will ultimately make all things new.
That is why our theme means so much to me.
Think about the people whose lives appear in Scripture.
David, whose adultery and abuse of royal power led to terrible consequences.
Peter, who denied the Lord he loved.
The Samaritan woman, whose personal history became part of a conversation that led her to speak about Jesus.
Paul, who once persecuted the church before becoming a servant of Christ.
Their stories are not identical.
Their sins, circumstances, and consequences are different.
And God's grace did not erase the historical reality of what happened.
But their failures did not have the final word over what God could do in their lives.
That is what I mean when I say Jesus rewrites everything.
Not that He makes the past imaginary.
Not that every earthly consequence disappears.
Not that repentance becomes optional.
But that through His death and resurrection, the future of a repentant sinner is no longer defined only by the shame of yesterday.
Listen to 2 Corinthians 5:17:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." — KJV
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means "new creation."
This is deeper than a temporary improvement in mood.
It speaks of the transforming reality of belonging to Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that today.
Your worst decision does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your secret sin does not have to remain your master.
Your history does not place you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
But neither can you simply rename your sin and call it grace.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness.
He does not ask us to pretend darkness is light.
He calls us out of darkness.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you have never told anyone, I want you to know why I keep writing.
Not because I have all the answers.
Not because I have reached some level of spiritual perfection.
Not because I believe my articles are indispensable.
I keep writing because the Gospel is too precious to remain unspoken.
Because Christ is worthy of being proclaimed.
Because people need more than shallow religious encouragement.
And because I believe God can use ordinary believers, ordinary words, and ordinary acts of obedience in ways we may never fully see.
Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 3:6:
"I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." — KJV
That verse protects my heart from something dangerous.
The temptation to believe that the results depend entirely on me.
They don't.
I can write.
I can study.
I can pray.
I can share.
I can correct my mistakes.
I can do everything possible to communicate the truth clearly and compassionately.
But I cannot manufacture spiritual transformation.
I cannot force someone to repent.
I cannot make a hardened heart believe.
I cannot convert a soul through emotional language, clever writing, or a perfect publishing schedule.
God gives the growth.
And that is freedom.
It means I do not need to manipulate your emotions to make my ministry look successful.
I do not need to claim that God told me you must read every word.
And I certainly do not need to turn financial support into a test of whether you truly love God.
The Gospel deserves better than that.
You deserve to hear the truth without pressure disguised as spiritual authority.
But I also want to speak openly about something important.
Gospel Warrior is not sustained by words alone.
There is work behind every article.
Time spent studying Scripture.
Time spent writing and editing.
Time spent preparing Christian resources.
Time spent maintaining a growing library and making discipleship materials available to people who may not have the money to purchase them.
Time spent trying to reach more readers with messages centered on Christ.
And as this work grows, so do the practical needs involved in sustaining and expanding it.
Not because God needs your money.
He doesn't.
Absolutely not.
I am inviting you because supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and partnership.
In Philippians 1:5, Paul thanks believers for their fellowship, or partnership, in the Gospel.
The Greek word κοινωνία (koinōnia) speaks of sharing or participation.
In context, Paul is grateful for the Philippians' continuing partnership in the work of the Gospel.
Later, in Philippians 4:15–18, he specifically acknowledges their material support.
That gives us a biblical foundation for voluntary financial partnership in Gospel work.
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and other genuine needs deserve prayerful consideration.
Not simply because it helps with expenses.
But because it allows this work to continue and, God willing, reach farther.
Perhaps to someone in another country.
Perhaps to someone who cannot afford a Christian book.
Perhaps to someone who has never opened a Bible but is willing to read a testimony.
Perhaps to a believer who has grown spiritually cold and needs to be reminded of the truth.
Only God knows what fruit may come.
But I can promise that the purpose of this ministry will remain the same.
To proclaim Jesus Christ.
To handle Scripture responsibly.
To call people toward repentance, faith, and spiritual growth.
To offer encouragement rooted in biblical truth.
And to continue making discipleship resources accessible.
And I want that word to remain meaningful.
FREE.
I know there are people who genuinely want to grow spiritually but are already struggling to provide for their families.
I see no reason to place unnecessary financial barriers between them and the biblical nourishment we can offer.
But I want to be clear about something.
It is not the Gospel.
Jesus is the reason this ministry exists.
Not because you are obligated to prove your faith publicly.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual rewards.
But because someone among your friends or family may need to hear the truth of the Gospel.
You may not know who.
Maybe the person who always reacts to your posts but never talks about their problems.
Maybe an old friend who has quietly walked away from church.
Maybe a relative who is carrying shame.
Maybe someone who thinks Christians have no room for people with a complicated past.
Sharing this article may give them an opportunity to encounter Scripture and consider Jesus.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their struggles.
But because you care about them.
You can even send it privately if that would be more thoughtful.
Not because my words deserve a permanent place in your heart.
But because the Scriptures discussed here deserve more than a hurried glance.
Return to them.
Read their surrounding chapters.
Examine what they mean.
Pray over what God is teaching you through His Word.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to follow as well.
They do not need to pretend to have everything figured out before they can begin learning about Jesus.
And there is one more thing I want to ask of you.
Not for an algorithm.
Not for another impressive engagement statistic.
But because I believe honest conversations can encourage people who think they are fighting their spiritual battles alone.
Not a polished religious answer.
Not something you think other Christians want to hear.
Just something true.
Perhaps your faith has been tired lately.
Perhaps you have been running from a conviction you know you need to face.
Perhaps you are grateful because Christ has carried you through a season you thought would destroy you.
Perhaps you are still learning how to pray again.
Or, if you need prayer, write:
You do not need to disclose anything private or painful that you are not ready to share publicly.
Someone else may be encouraged by hearing that another believer has struggled, repented, persevered, and continued following Christ.
Because the Christian life is not a performance in which everyone pretends to be strong.
It is a life of dependence on the Savior.
And that includes me.
There are days when I sit down to write and the words come slowly.
Days when I have to stop and search the Scriptures again.
Days when I realize that a sentence I thought was profound needs to be rewritten because it does not communicate the passage accurately.
Days when I have to surrender a topic I wanted to pursue and give attention to another concern that has become pressing through prayer, study, or the needs I see around me.
That is what I mean when I say I let the Holy Spirit guide my writing.
Not that I become unconscious of my choices.
Not that my judgment becomes infallible.
Not that careful study is unnecessary.
But that I want my decisions, including what to write about and when to stop, to be governed by prayerful submission to God and the authority of Scripture.
I am responsible for the words I publish.
And I remain accountable for correcting them when necessary.
That is part of honoring the Lord too.
Because spiritual sincerity without biblical accuracy can mislead people.
And biblical knowledge without love can wound people.
I want neither.
I want truth spoken in love.
I want grace that never excuses sin.
I want conviction that never hides the mercy of Christ.
I want writing that helps people open their Bibles rather than become dependent on my articles.
And I want every person who encounters Gospel Warrior to know that the invitation is ultimately not to follow me.
It is to follow Jesus.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who showed compassion to the broken.
The One who obeyed the Father perfectly.
The One who bore our sins upon the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One through whom forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered.
That Jesus.
Not a version of Him shaped to flatter our preferences.
Not a Jesus who exists merely to make our dreams come true.
The Jesus revealed in Scripture.
The Savior who calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
And perhaps that is why this article became longer than I initially expected.
Because I began by wanting to explain how I write.
But I cannot explain why I write without explaining whom I serve.
And I cannot explain whom I serve without telling you about the Gospel.
Because this ministry was never meant to be about the length of an article.
It was never meant to be about how many people recognize the Gospel Warrior name.
It was never meant to be about building a following large enough to impress the world.
I want to be faithful with what God has entrusted to me.
If one article is short, may it be faithful.
If another is long, may it be faithful.
If thousands read it, may Christ be glorified.
If only a few read it, may Christ still be glorified.
If someone is encouraged, may they thank the Lord.
If someone is convicted, may they turn toward Him.
If someone questions what I have written, may they search the Scriptures carefully.
And if someone finds an error, may I have the humility to receive correction.
Because this is not about defending my reputation.
It is about honoring the truth.
Before I finish, I want to return to the person I mentioned at the beginning.
The person I may never meet.
The person whose name I do not know.
The person I pray will encounter whatever truth from Scripture they need to hear.
Perhaps you are that person today.
I don't know.
I would never claim to know God's hidden purposes for your life simply because you encountered this article.
But I do know that the Gospel invitation is real.
You do not have to clean up your entire life before coming to Christ.
You come to Him in repentance and faith, trusting in His mercy and His finished work.
And the grace that receives sinners is also the grace that begins transforming them.
You may have a scandal in your past.
You may have wounds that still ache.
You may have consequences you cannot undo.
You may have years you wish you could recover.
But if you are in Christ, your story is not ultimately held together by your ability to repair every broken chapter.
It is held together by the Savior who redeems sinners.
If Jesus is calling you to stop hiding, to repent, to trust Him, or to return to a life of faithful obedience, what are you waiting for?
Don't answer that for me.
Answer it before God.

You can also help this message reach others by sharing it, tagging someone who would appreciate its encouragement, saving it for deeper reflection, and following Gospel Warrior for more Christ-centered teaching.
May you know Jesus Christ.
May you grow in the truth of His Word.
May you experience the freedom of repentance and forgiveness.
May you learn to recognize His grace without taking His holiness lightly.
And may your life become a testimony that points others toward Him.
Tomorrow, I may sit down to write again.
I may have a subject already on my heart.
Or I may discover, through prayer, study, and the needs before me, that I need to write about something entirely different.
I may write a few paragraphs.
I may write several pages.
But before I begin, I hope to offer the same prayer I have offered so many times.

"Lord, please guide my words. Keep me faithful to Scripture. Guard me from pride and error. Let Jesus be glorified. And if someone needs to encounter Your truth through this message, please open the door for it to reach them."
Then I will write.
And when the article is finished, I will place the outcome in God's hands.
Because the greatest thing that could ever happen through Gospel Warrior is not that someone becomes a fan of my writing.
It is that someone comes to know and follow Jesus Christ.
If you remember nothing else about the person behind these articles, remember the Savior I have spent every word trying to point you toward.
